headings: ## 4. What You Want From Your Character
text: Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 1 Your Character Guide A workbook for the Salt Road party · Fill it in, hand it to Claude, get back your own guide: levelling plan, combat cheat sheet, role-play help and DM notes. How this works, in 3 steps 1. Fill in what you can. Type straight into the boxes, or print it and write. 2. Give it to Claude (claude.ai) with your D&D Beyond link, and paste the prompt from the last page. 3. Claude builds your guide. Ask it for changes until you like it. Come back and update it when you level up. The ground rules • Nothing here is required. Skip any box. Claude will work with whatever you give it and ask about the gaps. • Bullet points and half-sentences are fine. “grumpy, loves cheese, hates boats” is a perfectly good answer. • No order needed. Start wherever you like. Come back later. Do it over several sittings. • Stuck on a box? Leave it blank and write “help me with this” instead. That’s a great thing to give Claude. The Short Version Only got 10 minutes? Do these three and you’ll already get a useful guide: Do this Section ☐ Paste your D&D Beyond link (and set the character to Public) 1 ☐ Paste your backstory, even a rough one 3 ☐ Tick what you want from your character, and what you find hard 4 Progress Tracker Tick sections off as you go. Tick “skipped” too: skipping is a valid choice. Section Time Section Time ☐ 1. The basics 3 min ☐ 8. The people in your life 5 min ☐ 2. The one-line pitch 3 min ☐ 9. You and the party 10 min ☐ 3. Backstory 5 min ☐ 10. Running gags & side projects 5 min ☐ 4. What you want 5 min ☐ 11. In combat 5 min ☐ 5. Build & levelling 5 min ☐ 12. Hooks, secrets & limits 5 min ☐ 6. Skills & what you’re good at 3 min ☐ 13. Questions for the DM 3 min ☐ 7. Personality & voice 10 min ☐ 14. Hand it to Claude 2 min What you get back. The same kind of guide Mossy’s player has: a quick-start summary, a combat cheat sheet for your current level, a levelling plan, how to play your character (especially in party scenes), your relationships with each teammate, and a DM notes section with story hooks. You can also ask for a short party handout (no spoilers) and a separate DM brief.

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 2 1. The Basics Time: about 3 min Why: the character sheet does most of the work. Claude can read your D&D Beyond character directly, so it knows your stats, spells, items and features without you typing them out. Character name Player name (and what to call you) Race / class / subclass / level (e.g. “Human Gunslinger, High Roller, level 3”) D&D Beyond link (e.g. https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/12345678) Make your character readable first On D&D Beyond: open your character → Manage (or the gear icon) → Character Settings → Character Privacy → Public. Without this, Claude can’t open the link. It only makes the sheet viewable, not editable. 2. The One-Line Pitch Time: about 3 min · Skip if: you really can’t think of one. Claude can suggest a few from your backstory. Why: one sentence gives Claude (and you) a compass. Every time you’re unsure what your character would do, you can check it against this. Try one of these formulas:  [Famous character] meets [another famous character].  A [adjective] [role] who wants [goal] but [problem].  [Character] if they were [job / situation]. Your pitch Meet Mossy Thistlewick, our made-up example character for this workbook (she’s not in the party). A gnome Circle of Spores Druid: a former royal food-taster, now a dungeon mushroom forager. Example (Mossy): “Mary Poppins meets Gordon Ramsay”: a cheerful, bossy nanny type who judges everyone’s cooking.

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 3 3. Backstory Time: about 5 min Why: this is where DM hooks and role-play ideas come from. Even a messy paragraph gives Claude a lot to work with.  Paste your backstory as it is. Long, short, or bullet points.  If you have two versions (a short one the party knows and a longer private one), paste both and say which is which.  Unfinished? That’s fine. Write what you know and put “TBD” on the rest. Backstory (or where to find it, e.g. “it’s on my D&D Beyond sheet”) What the rest of the party already knows about you What the party doesn’t know yet (secrets). Goes in your DM notes only Example (Mossy): The party knows she was sacked from the royal kitchens after a lord was poisoned at a banquet. They don’t know that she was the one who poisoned him, or why. 4. What You Want From Your Character Time: about 5 min Why: a guide should be built around what you find fun and what you find hard, not just what’s mathematically strongest. In combat, I mostly want to… (tick any) Deal big damage Hit lots of enemies at once Heal and protect Tank / hold the line Control the battlefield Buff my allies Be sneaky / scout Be the face in talks Solve puzzles / utility Be hard to kill Do cool stunts Not sure yet I find these hard… (tick any. This is the most useful box in the workbook)

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 4 Knowing what to say in party chat Talking to NPCs Deciding what to do on my turn Remembering my abilities Keeping track of resources Staying in character Knowing when to speak up Picking spells / feats Rules and edge cases Remembering the story so far Making decisions quickly Nothing in particular Anything else you want from this character (a story arc, a vibe, a moment you’re hoping for) Example (Mossy): Control first, support second. Wants a slow arc about forgiving herself. Finds talking to NPCs the hardest part, so the guide gives her “go-to moves” to use when she’s stuck. 5. Build & Levelling Time: about 5 min · Skip if: you’d rather Claude suggest a plan from scratch. Just tick the first box. Why: Claude can plan your next levels, check your choices against the house rules, and turn it all into a one-page cheat sheet. Suggest a plan for me I have a plan, check it I have a guide/video I’m following Keep it simple Optimise hard Flavour over power Your plan, or a link / name of the build you’re following Choices you’re unsure about (spells, feats, multiclassing, items) Example (Mossy): Following a Spores Druid build from a YouTube guide. Unsure whether to take War Caster or Resilient (CON) first. 6. Skills & What You’re Good At Time: about 3 min Why: most of the game isn’t combat. Knowing your best skills tells you when to step forward. Your top 3 skills or tools, and when they matter (e.g. “Stealth: scouting ahead”) Things only you in the party can do

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 5 Things you’re bad at (useful for funny or dramatic moments) 7. Personality & Voice Time: about 10 min · Skip if: you’d rather describe the vibe and let Claude write the rest. Why: this becomes the “how to play them” part of your guide: ready-made lines and reactions you can reach for mid-session. Prompt Example (Mossy) Trait Something people notice within five minutes Tastes everything first, including things she really shouldn’t Ideal What they believe in “Nobody fights well on an empty stomach.” Bond Who or what they’d fight for Old Mother Cap, the talking mushroom who taught her magic Flaw What gets them in trouble Can’t resist fixing other people’s food, or lives Traits, ideals, bonds, flaws How they talk (accent, speed, favourite words, nicknames for people) 2–3 catchphrases or things they’d say Idea to steal: “modes”. Most characters switch between a few modes. Name 2–3 and write when each one shows up. When you’re stuck in a scene, just pick the mode that fits. Mossy has Nanny (default: bossy and caring), The Critic (any time food is involved) and Quiet Mossy (rare: something scares her, and the chatter stops). Your character’s modes (optional)

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 6 8. The People in Your Life Time: about 5 min · Skip if: your backstory already covers it. Why: NPCs are the DM’s easiest hooks. Every name you give is a story waiting to happen. Family, mentors, rivals, enemies, patrons, gods, exes, debts. Name + one line on each Example (Mossy): Lord Hallowmere, the noble who was poisoned (and survived). Chef Barrow, her old boss, who fired her. Old Mother Cap, the talking mushroom who taught her druid magic. 9. You and the Party Time: about 10 min Why: party scenes are where most people get stuck. A clear idea of how you feel about each teammate gives you something to say. Your teammates. Their D&D Beyond links are included so Claude can read their sheets too. Character What we know D&D Beyond Mossy Thistlewick Gnome Spores Druid. Forages mushrooms, feeds everyone dndbeyond.com/characters/1 1111111 Ash Vale Human Fighter dndbeyond.com/characters/2 2222222 Cinder Moss Tiefling Warlock dndbeyond.com/characters/4 4444444 For each teammate (skip yourself), answer any of these:  What do you think of them? (Trust, annoyed by, impressed by, protective of, suspicious of…)  What would you tease them about? What would you ask them?  What could you do together in a fight? (Combos, protecting each other, covering weaknesses) Mossy Ash Cinder Example (Mossy): Mossy treats her party’s barbarian like a child who needs feeding: she packs them labelled lunches, and takes it personally when they eat monster meat instead.

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 7 10. Running Gags & Side Projects Time: about 5 min · Skip if: nothing comes to mind. These often appear on their own after a few sessions. Why: a recurring bit gives you something to do in every scene without having to think of something new. A habit, an object, a catchphrase or a bit you keep coming back to Something they do in downtime (a job, a hobby, a scheme, a project) Example (Mossy): The star ratings: she rates every meal the party eats out of five, out loud, including the ones cooked by enemies. In downtime she sells “dungeon-safe” mushroom jerky. 11. In Combat Time: about 5 min Why: your cheat sheet will list your best move for each situation, so you’re not scrolling through your sheet when it’s your turn. What do you usually do on your turn right now? What do you use your bonus action and reaction for? (or “I always forget I have them”) Situations where you’re not sure what to do Flanking is on. Potions are a bonus action.

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 8 12. Hooks, Secrets & Limits Time: about 5 min Why: this becomes the DM notes section. It helps the DM give your character story moments you’ll actually enjoy. Story moments you’d love to see (a reunion, a rival, a reveal, a big choice) Where you’d like the character to end up (redemption, revenge, power, home, a surprise) Things you’d rather avoid in your character’s story (topics, situations, anything) Example (Mossy): Would love: Lord Hallowmere turning up in Brinemarket, and a teammate finding out a big secret from her past. 13. Questions for the DM Time: about 3 min · Skip if: you have none. You can always add them later. Why: writing down rules questions stops them getting lost, and the guide can track the answers. Anything you’re unsure about (house rules, how a feature works here, anything unclear) Campaign Facts (so Claude gets them right) Rests Standard Levelling Milestone

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 9 14. Hand It to Claude First: What Claude Needs (one time, 2 minutes) These are the only things used to make the guides. No plugins or extra add-ons. Claude needs to… What to do Read your character Set your D&D Beyond character to Public (section 1) and include the link Open links and look up lore Claude chat: Settings → Capabilities → turn on web search. Claude Code: nothing to do Make and check the PDF Claude chat: Settings → Capabilities → turn on code execution and file creation. Claude Code: nothing to do Know the house rules Attach the campaign’s character creation guide (PDF) if you have it. Ask the DM for a copy if not Then: Paste the Prompt Start a new chat in Claude (or a new Claude Code session), attach this filled-in PDF (or paste your answers), and copy in the prompt below. Change anything in [brackets]. I play [character name] in The Salt Road, a caravan campaign. I've attached my filled-in character workbook. My character: https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/[your ID] (If you can't open that page, try: https://character-service.dndbeyond.com/character/v5/character/[your ID] ) My party (read their sheets too): Mossy Thistlewick https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/11111111 Ash Vale https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/22222222 Cinder Moss https://www.dndbeyond.com/characters/44444444 Please make me a character guide as a PDF, with: 1. A one-page summary of who my character is and where I am now 2. A combat cheat sheet for my current level (action, bonus action, reaction), including where I'm fighting on the salt flats 3. A levelling plan for the next few levels, with reasons 4. How to play my character: personality, voice, example lines, and go-to moves for when I'm stuck in a scene 5. My relationship with each teammate, with ideas for scenes 6. Party tactics: combos and how we cover each other 7. DM notes: key NPCs, story hooks, my secrets, open questions How to build it: - Read my sheet, and the campaign guide if I've attached it. Where they disagree, follow my sheet and list it as a question for the DM. - Only use content the campaign allows (no homebrew races). - Give your own recommendations with reasons, even if they differ from any build guide I mention. - If a rule is unclear, write your assumption and mark it 'check with DM'. Don't invent things the DM decides: leave [placeholders]. - Look up setting lore only where it helps role-play or DM hooks. Layout: - A4, clear headings, and the same structure in every section. - A TL;DR at the top. Short sentences, one idea per bullet, tables instead of long paragraphs, bold key words, plain language. Explain any jargon the first time it appears. - Put the combat cheat sheet on its own page(s) so I can print it. - British English. - Before giving me the PDF, render each page and check for cut-off text, headings stranded at the bottom of a page, and big gaps. Ask me about anything missing before you guess.

Your Character Guide — Workbook · updated 28 Sep 2026 Page 10 One More: All Three PDFs at Once Want the full set, like Mossy’s player has? Use this after the main prompt (or instead of it): Using my workbook and the D&D Beyond links, create THREE separate PDFs, all in the same style: 1. PERSONAL GUIDE: everything, for me. Summary, combat cheat sheet, levelling plan, how to play my character, teammates, tactics, DM notes and open questions. 2. PARTY HANDOUT (2-3 pages): safe to share with the group. Who my character is (only what the party already knows), what they can do for the party, and easy ways to play off them. Leave out my secrets, DM notes and anything that would spoil a future story moment between characters. 3. DM BRIEF: for my DM. What the party knows vs what they don't, my secrets, key NPCs, my arc, story hooks, what I want from the character, things I'd rather avoid, and my open rules questions. In the party handout, no hints either: examples, catchphrases and jokes mustn't point at a secret. Follow the same build and layout rules as above. Before you start, tell me which of my details you're treating as secret, so I can check nothing spoilery ends up in the party handout. Useful Follow-Ups Once you have your guide, you can ask Claude for more. Copy any of these: Ask for Prompt A party overview “Read all three D&D Beyond links and give me a party overview: who does what, gaps we have, and combos between us.” A party handout “Make a 2-page handout I can share with my party. Nothing from my secrets or DM notes.” A DM brief “Make a separate brief for my DM with my hooks, secrets, arc and open rules questions.” Help in the moment “My character just [situation]. Give me three things they might say.” Level-up “I just hit level [X]. Update my cheat sheet and levelling plan.” After a session “Here’s what happened last session: […]. Update my guide and suggest new hooks.” A teammate scene “Give me an in-character conversation starter between my character and [teammate].” Keep this workbook. When your character changes (new level, big story moment, new backstory reveal), update the relevant box and ask Claude to update your guide. Small, frequent updates are easier than one big one.
